clinicalPearls: A true osteonecrosis of the tarsal navicular occurring in the immature foot, not a traction apophysitis
Affected bone is the tarsal navicular, the last tarsal bone to ossify, which is vulnerable during its ossification
Typically affects children aged around four to seven years and is more common in boys
Presents with a painful limp, tenderness and sometimes swelling over the medial midfoot, with weight-bearing on the outer border of the foot
The radiographic hallmark is a flattened, sclerotic and fragmented navicular with narrowing of the ossific nucleus
Frequently unilateral, though it can be bilateral, and radiographic changes may lag or persist behind clinical improvement
It is a self-limiting condition, with the navicular typically reconstituting to a normal or near-normal shape over time
Management is supportive with offloading, activity modification and short-term immobilisation for symptom relief as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Kohler disease is an osteochondrosis of the tarsal navicular caused by temporary interruption of its blood supply during a vulnerable period of ossification. Because the navicular is the last tarsal bone to ossify and lies at the apex of the medial longitudinal arch, it is subjected to compressive forces at a time when its single ossific nucleus and vascular supply are still immature. Transient ischaemia leads to sclerosis, flattening and fragmentation of the developing bone, which is often exacerbated by weight-bearing stress. Because the vascular insult is temporary and the child continues to grow, revascularisation and remodelling usually restore normal or near-normal navicular architecture, distinguishing it from the adult navicular osteonecrosis of Mueller-Weiss syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Septic arthritis or osteomyelitis of the midfoot
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis of the midfoot
Normal irregular or multicentric ossification of the navicular
additionalInvestigations: Weight-bearing foot radiographs demonstrating navicular sclerosis, flattening and fragmentation
Comparison views of the contralateral foot to distinguish disease from normal ossification variation
Magnetic resonance imaging where the diagnosis is uncertain or infection is suspected
Inflammatory markers and full blood count if septic arthritis or osteomyelitis is a concern
Clinical assessment of gait and site of maximal tenderness over the medial midfoot
Follow-up radiographs to document reconstitution of the navicular
redFlags: Fever, marked swelling or systemic upset suggesting infection rather than osteochondrosis
Rest pain or night pain raising concern for an alternative pathology
Failure of symptoms to settle over the expected course prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
Bilateral or atypical disease warranting consideration of a systemic condition
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; Kohler disease is self-limiting and the navicular almost always reconstitutes to normal shape with resolution of symptoms, typically within months to a couple of years and without long-term sequelae.
pitfalls: Mistaking normal irregular navicular ossification for disease and over-investigating an asymptomatic child
Failing to consider infection when swelling, warmth or systemic features are present
Confusing the benign childhood condition with the more serious adult Mueller-Weiss navicular osteonecrosis
Prolonged unnecessary immobilisation given the naturally self-limiting course
management: Reassurance, as the navicular osteochondrosis is self-limiting with an excellent prognosis and near-universal reconstitution of the bone
Simple analgesia and activity or weight-bearing modification for pain
A short-leg walking cast or immobilisation for a period in more painful cases to hasten symptom relief
Medial arch support or orthoses for comfort once immobilisation is discontinued
Avoidance of surgery, which is not indicated
Clinical and radiographic follow-up to confirm reconstitution, recognising radiographic change lags behind clinical improvement

Escalate: exclude septic arthritis or osteomyelitis with inflammatory markers and MRI
Weight-bearing foot radiographs, contralateral views, MRI if uncertain
Do radiographs show a flattened, sclerotic and fragmented navicular?
